results.title: The AI Capex Boom, Revisited: Is Capital scarcity about to meet Compute excess?
highlights:
1. that AI demand is effectively unlimited, and that the binding constraint is a shortage of compute so acute that anyone who builds capacity will be able to rent it at a profit.
2. The capex was justified because the chips were scarce and the scarcity was permanent.

...

The single most repeated justification for the buildout of compute capacity is scarcity. We are told the world cannot make enough GPUs, that every chip is spoken for, that hyperscalers are “compute constrained” and that we need to build an endless number of new datacenters to accommodate AI’s current, let alone future, demand. Take that as given and the capex might make sense if you are a bull on pricing (ie no sensitivity): you are racing to own a scarce, rentable asset.

The problem is that the scarcity narrative is now being contradicted by the behaviour of the very companies that should be the most compute-starved. In addition, new solutions are emerging that increase capacity not through additional chips but through a combination of introducing marketability and transparency which can raise actual utilisation rates. And these initiatives are happening before western companies start deploying the techniques and tools of their Chinese peers which have operated with constraints for years now.

...

In May 2026, xAI signed Anthropic to take all of Colossus 1, its Memphis supercomputer data center: more than 220,000 Nvidia GPUs and roughly 300 megawatts, for about $1.25 billion a month through 2029. A month later a separate filing showed Google taking a similar deal at roughly $920 million a month for around 110,000 GPUs, also running to mid-2029. Combined, that is in the region of $26 billion a year of compute rented out by a frontier lab to two of its best-funded competitors.

So xAI which is supposedly in an existential race for compute and building a second campus (Colossus 2) at enormous expense, has concluded that the most profitable use of its first data center is to lease it to the competition. The reported reason is revealing: Colossus 1’s mixed H100 / H200 / GB200 fleet made efficient large-scale training awkward. A reported internal xAI memo put Colossus 1’s Model FLOPs Utilization, a measure of how much of the hardware’s theoretical compute was actually used, at around 11 percent, against 35 to 45 percent for production-grade training, a level the memo itself reportedly called ‘embarrassingly low.’ xAI did not have too little compute, it had a large, underutilized asset it could not run efficiently, so it became a landlord.

...

How good a business is being a compute landlord? (and the oddity of these deals) xAI has not disclosed Colossus 1’s build price, but a bottom-up estimate is tractable: roughly 220,000 GPUs at an all-in $30,000 to $45,000 each (silicon plus servers, networking and racks) is around $7 to $10 billion, and a 300 MW shell with electrical and cooling adds perhaps $3 to $4.5 billion. Call it $12 to $16 billion (equating to $40-53bn / GW). Against that, Anthropic alone is paying about $1.25 billion a month, or roughly $15 billion a year, to rent the machine. On that basis the asset pays back its entire construction cost in something like twelve to eighteen months, an unlevered cash yield on cost of around 90 to 125 percent before depreciation, and operating cost (power) runs at barely 1 percent of revenue.

...

That is a large hidden capacity reserve. If capex plans are implicitly anchored to low realized utilization, then simply using the existing machines better can delay, shrink, or cancel a large share of forecast chip purchases even while end-demand keeps rising. xAI’s 11 percent figure may be an outlier but it is also a live example of the reserve the note describes.

...

What makes this an inflection rather than teething trouble is the pincer it creates for the model layer. The input cost firmed through 2026 rather than collapsing: independent GPU-rental indices show H100 rates up roughly 20 to 30 percent year-to-April, to about $2.40 to $2.64 per GPU-hour, with H200, B200 and B300 all higher too, before peaking in spring and beginning to roll over as shown in the chart above which ends in May. At the same time, competition is forcing the labs to cut what they charge: in June, OpenAI was reported to be weighing “drastic” reductions to its token prices to defend share against Anthropic, whose Claude Code tool had gone viral and whose valuation had briefly overtaken it. Bloomberg’s understatement is the whole point: such cuts “could erode the profit margins of both companies, which already lose billions.” Sam Altman, who said at the start of 2026 that “the cost issue never came up,” now calls cost “a huge issue.”

...

The rental market has lately become the cleanest live test of all this, and it cuts in two directions. On one hand, the steep-depreciation bears have been wrong so far: if GPUs were obsolete in two years their rental rates should be in freefall, yet SiliconData’s indices (via 3Fourteen Research) put the A100’s decline at roughly 16 percent a year, the H100’s at about 4 percent and the B200’s at about 2 percent, far shallower than a two-year write-down implies. A separate Architect index sharpens the point: the H100, the oldest model with the largest installed base, shows the highest year-to-date rental increase of all, up about 30 percent at its peak. Residual values are holding, which is exactly what the neoclouds’ asset-backed financing needs, and it is a genuine mark against the bear case. However, these data likely reflect the tokenmaxxing through the first 3-4 months discussed in the previous segment and are thus out of date and have since reversed sharply.

Indeed, on the other hand, those same prices firmed into a spring 2026 peak and have just begun to roll over, possibly the more crucial signal. As the head of Goldman’s Delta One desk put it, “the most important metric remains compute rental prices... If supply rises and rental prices continue to drift lower, that is a direct challenge to the shortage narrative. The first place that pain shows up is hardware.” He flagged the ORNN H100 index “rolling over” as worth watching and located the real risk “upstream in the hardware and infrastructure stack where expectations remain built around persistent scarcity.” Architect’s twelve-month GPU future already trades about 28 percent below spot. So the rental tape is, for now, kinder to the neoclouds’ balance sheets than the bears feared, but it is turning at precisely the layer where the most scarcity is priced in. We would add only that the same desk’s faith in the hyperscalers as the safe harbour sits awkwardly with the capex and free-cash-flow math in Part 5: in our view the rollover is a warning for the whole stack, not just the silicon.

...

We have at the same time both shortages and clear bottlenecks, as well as oversupply and more efficient solutions that are ... We have record investment and what looks like a potential capital constraint. xAI can lease compute at a premium, which says capacity is scarce and valuable; the token-price index is falling, which says the output is commoditising; enterprises are rationing, which says demand is soft; and the pipeline shows another wave of capacity still being built. Bulls have seized on the first of these, and the argument doing the rounds is that if the xAI/SpaceX price is the true clearing price for compute, the listed neoclouds are cheap and have upside. It is worth resolving the apparent contradiction head-on, because the resolution is the whole thesis in miniature.

...

So the bull syllogism breaks at three joints. First, the xAI price may not be a clean market price at all: roughly $1.25 billion a month for about 220,000 GPUs works out near $7 to $8 per GPU-hour, some three times neocloud spot and contract rates, on deals struck inside a circular Nvidia-Anthropic-Google-xAI web and just ahead of a SpaceX listing. Valuing arm’s-length neoclouds off a possibly related-party, pre-IPO print is shaky. Second, the scarcity it reflects is an assumed (by the hyperscalers building ahead) today bottleneck of warm shells and power, not silicon, and the pipeline below shows a 2026-2028 supply wave landing into exactly that bottleneck, while utilization and efficiency tools lift effective supply with no new boxes. Capitalising a spot scarcity price near the top of a build cycle is the classic late-cycle error. Third, and decisively, a lease is only as good as the tenant’s economics, and the falling token price is the leading indicator of those economics: output down twenty percent while the flagship lab already loses $1.60 per dollar of revenue makes the rents harder to service, not easier. That is Chamath’s own warning made concrete in the Crusoe pause.

...

Step back, and the cross-currents stop looking contradictory and start to rhyme. Strong demand in places, rationing in others, a shortage now and a glut arriving, capital reaching into ever more currencies to fund the build: taken one at a time they appear to cancel out, but together they are the signature of a capital cycle topping rather than an early-cycle boom. Early in a cycle the price of the output rises with demand and capacity chases it.

results.title: Compute Is the New Oil. So Who Builds the Drilling Rigs?
highlights:
In the same month, CME and ICE both announced compute futures tied to GPU rental rate indices, and compute began turning into a cash-settled exchange commodity.[1][2] Put SpaceX’s Cursor acquisition, the Oracle-OpenAI $300B/4.5GW deal, and Microsoft-OpenAI’s end of exclusivity in one frame, and the unit the market prices is shifting from chip ASP to contracted compute.[3][4][5] The thesis here is simple. Contracting GW eventually translates into wafer starts one layer down, and no matter who wins at the chip and compute layer, the supplier-agnostic layer everyone passes through is deposition, etch, bonding, probe, burn-in, ATE, and metrology. If compute is oil, part of the money is made not at the oilfield but in the rigs that drill it and the tools that inspect it.

...

The same exchanges that trade crude, corn, and bitcoin are now moving to list compute. In May, CME partnered with Silicon Data to announce compute futures based on a GPU on-demand rental rate index, set to launch later this year and pending regulatory review.[1] The contracts are cash-settled rather than physically delivered, and days later ICE brought its own GPU futures based on Ornn’s Compute Price Index, so the two largest exchanges moved the same way in the same week.[2] CME called compute the new oil of the 21st century.[1]

...

Compute financialization also speeds this up. The exchanges describe the futures market as a way to give data centers price protection.[2] Once a forward curve exists, GW buildout becomes bankable, easier financing means faster expansion, and faster expansion means more wafer starts. The fact that this buildout is currently supply-constrained by material and labor shortages, with reports of some Oracle-linked OpenAI data centers slipping toward 2028 even as Oracle says its contractual milestones remain on track,[6] is exactly what makes price protection through a forward curve meaningful. Making compute a commodity grows demand for the equipment that produces that commodity.

results.title: The case for a GPU Futures Market - kerem's Substack
highlights: Silicon Data is the first part of the piece. While the name of this company does not dominate the headlines as much as the other household names when it comes to AI, it is quietly designing the solutions that seek to solve the bottleneck to plug AI supply chain into the financial exchanges. You can think of it like a Bloomberg for all things chips. Think of the benchmarking functions Bloomberg does for other securities applied for the security that would be AI compute. It tracks the costs to rent GPUs like NVIDIA A100, H100, B200, etc., across providers and regions. It then standardizes it into an index á la S&P . Its GPU Index gives daily standardized rental-price data and historical time series for procurement, investment, and cloud-cost benchmarking. So the implication of all this is that, you end up with AI compute looking a lot like any other tradable commodity on the market. Complete with all the GPU forward curves that would revolutionize the GPU rental pricing over a 36-month horizon.

results.title: The Neocloud Cartel: How the AI Industry Started Renting Compute From Itself - Thorsten Meyer AI
highlights:
They rent. They rent from a new class of GPU landlords that didn’t exist three years ago. They rent, increasingly, from each other — Anthropic now trains on xAI’s supercomputer, paying a competitor over a billion dollars a month. And the money they spend renting loops, with remarkable consistency, back to a single chip maker that has quietly become an investor in nearly everyone at the table.

...

~$3T datacenter spend ’25–’28 — half on private credit

−$74B OpenAI projected operating loss, 2028

~3% of consumers actually pay for AI

−60–75% H100 rental rates from peak — commoditizing

...

The cartel isn’t a conspiracy — it’s the endpoint of extreme capital intensity, real scarcity, and one dominant supplier. But the same circularity that makes it powerful makes it a fuse: each cancelled order is someone else’s missing revenue. Don’t be a price-taker at the bottom of a loop you don’t control — own your inference, keep an open-weight fallback, diversify silicon.

...

The category has an ugly name — “neocloud” — and a simple definition: an AI-only hyperscaler, GPU-as-a-service without the legacy baggage of a general-purpose cloud. It exists because the 2024–25 GPU shortage left even well-funded labs on months-long waitlists, and renting was the only way to get to scale without spending four years building.

...

Then, in May 2026, the category gained its most surprising member. xAI — an integrated frontier lab, the kind whose whole strategy argues against handing capacity to rivals — leased its Colossus 1 supercomputer to Anthropic for about $1.25 billion a month and to Google for about $920 million a month, roughly $26 billion a year, because its own Grok training had moved elsewhere and the cluster was sitting at an embarrassing 11% utilization. When even a self-described full-stack lab becomes a landlord, the message is unmistakable: in 2026, compute is something you rent, and ownership has decoupled from use.

...

A loop where suppliers finance customers who buy from suppliers works beautifully while demand and stock prices rise — each leg validates the next. It works in reverse just as efficiently. Morgan Stanley pegs global data-center spending at roughly $3 trillion between 2025 and 2028, about half of it funded by private credit. OpenAI is reportedly on track for a $74 billion operating loss in 2028; one estimate puts its cumulative losses near $140 billion across 2024–29. And the end demand that’s supposed to justify all of it is thin: by one count, only about 3% of consumers pay for AI, perhaps $12 billion a year, against trillions in committed capex. Meanwhile H100 rental rates have fallen 60–75% from their peak — the clearest possible signal that the scarce thing is commoditizing.

results.title: Why colos are moving up the stack into bare metal and GPUaaS | Telecom Ramblings
highlights:
Power is the binding constraint on new GPU deployments. Operators who already hold energized space are looking to convert compute demand into revenue themselves. Colocation facilities and former bitcoin miners are moving up the stack into bare metal and GPU-as-a-Service. And colocation facilities can finance the climb on better terms than the new neoclouds they compete with.

...

North America’s data center vacancy ended 2025 at 1.4%, a record low, with three quarters of capacity under construction already preleased. New supply is gated by the grid. Transformers take two and a half years, high-voltage substations three to five, and only 13% of what entered US interconnection queues between 2000 and 2019 ever got built.

“Time to power” is a defining success metric for many GPU operators. This makes it natural for colocation facilities to consider providing bare metal themselves. If you have space, it seems feasible to buy and rack GPU servers, and rent them out whole.

The catch is CapEx. GPU servers are more expensive than the infrastructure that house them. IREN needs to buy $5.8 billion of hardware from Dell to fill its 200 megawatts. The payback on typical GPU projects is around 24 to 30 months. If the AI bubble pops at 30 months, or rental rates drop, you might never turn a profit on the equipment.

...

Lenders split an AI data center into two assets on different clocks. The shell gets real estate debt over 15 to 20 years. The chips get their own loans over three to four years.

GPU-backed debt is expensive. CoreWeave’s first facility was priced around 15% in 2023, its second near 11%, and no GPU loan reached investment grade until March 2026. Data center real estate has been investment-grade collateral since 2018 and produced $25 billion of securitizations in 2025.

results.title: Is Frontier AI a Software Play?
highlights: AI infrastructure investment in 2025 and 2026 absorbed $222 billion of U.S. venture capital, representing 65.6 percent of all domestic deal value, as GPU cloud operators, data center developers, and electrical grid companies replaced software startups as the primary destination for institutional capital. The critical constraint on further deployment is not GPU supply or investor appetite: it is electricity. Transformer delivery times now extend three to five years, and switchgear is sold out through 2028, creating a bottleneck that is delaying or cancelling 30 to 50 percent of large data centers scheduled for completion in 2026.

results.title: To Solve Compute Availability, Be a Marriott, Not an Airbnb
highlights:
The AI compute shortage has a well kept secret. While startups wait months for GPU allocations and researchers abandon experiments because cloud bills are prohibitive, thousands of H100s sit idle in data centers between training runs — burning power and generating zero revenue for their owners.

Both things are true simultaneously, and that gap is a business.

...

The loudest narrative in AI infrastructure is that there aren’t enough GPUs. That’s partially right. There aren’t enough GPUs at the terms most people can actually access them on.

CoreWeave — the largest neocloud — requires 2–5 year commitments with take-or-pay penalties and upfront deposits of 15–25% of contract value. AWS charges $8+/hr for H100s and routes customers through an enterprise sales process. Neither was built for the researcher who needs 256 GPUs for three weeks, or the seed-stage startup that can’t sign a $10M multi-year contract.

This isn’t a shortage of chips. It’s a distribution problem. The compute exists. The terms under which it’s available exclude the majority of people who need it.

...

Idle GPU time is everywhere once you know where to look:

- AI labs run training jobs that last weeks, then sit idle during evaluation, debugging, and internal review before the next run begins
- Companies that over-contracted during the 2023 GPU frenzy are hemorrhaging cash on reservations they can’t fully utilize
- Data centers that built clusters to win anchor tenants are running at 50–60% utilization while their sales pipeline catches up to their capex

A conservative estimate: 20–30% of deployed H100 capacity sits idle at any given moment. At today’s fleet sizes, that’s tens of thousands of GPUs generating no revenue for owners and no value for the builders who need them. The supply exists. It just has no plumbing.

...

The natural instinct is to build a pure marketplace. Aggregate idle supply, connect it to demand, take a spread. Capital-light, scalable, elegant.

This is what Vast.ai tried. Their peer-to-peer marketplace lists GPUs from individual owners — data centers, crypto miners, research institutions, even personal machines. Prices are low: an A100 80GB can be had for under $0.70/hr vs $1.19/hr on a managed platform.

The problem is reliability. A misconfigured InfiniBand fabric, a node that drops mid-job, inconsistent power from a secondary data center — none of this shows up in a listing. It shows up 47 hours into a training run when your checkpoint is corrupted and your experiment is lost. A bad night in an Airbnb is recoverable. A failed training run is not.

Unverified, heterogeneous supply cannot support a single market-clearing price. You end up with a listing site like eBay, not a true exchange. Sophisticated buyers treat it as a sandbox for experiments, not a platform for production.

...

A 1,000 H100 cluster costs roughly $40M in capex — hardware, InfiniBand networking, data center buildout. At $1.96/hr per GPU and 70% utilization, that’s approximately $12M in annual revenue. Three-year payback, before financing costs, power, and staff. CoreWeave solved this by raising $30 billion in GPU-backed debt, with NVIDIA itself as an equity holder. That path is closed for a startup.

...

Marriott doesn’t own most of its hotels. It sets the standard, runs the distribution, and collects a management fee while franchisees own the physical assets. Applied to GPU compute, three business motions make this work:

Property management. Take operational control of third-party clusters. The hardware owner spent the capex; you provide the software layer, customer acquisition, SLAs, and 24/7 support. You earn a management fee on assets you don’t own. Zero capex on those clusters, recurring revenue.

Take-or-pay with customer deposits. When a customer commits to a long-term reservation, collect 15–25% upfront and build the capacity against that signed contract. The customer funds the build before hardware is purchased. You’re not speculating on demand — you’re fulfilling pre-sold capacity.

The order book. Let customers who aren’t using their contracted capacity list it back into the marketplace. The same GPU generates revenue twice — once through the primary contract, again through the sublease spread. Effective utilization moves from 70% toward 85%+. That 15-point improvement compresses the payback period significantly and makes the unit economics viable without a CoreWeave-scale balance sheet.

results.title: GPU-as-a-Service & Neocloud: Examining the Supply Chain for Artificial Intelligence
highlights:
### The AI supply chain - the "compute stack"

 The AI supply chain is a layered ecosystem underpinned by digital infrastructure. At present, demand for advanced compute exceeds supply. Expansion in supply to meet that demand is constrained by power availability, grid connection, cooling (hence water availability), network capacity, data-centre space, capital, and the need for specialised engineering. A shortage in any one of those inputs could constrain ultimate supply of AI to end users in the coming years. 

 The compute stack 

 Specifically, an AI service may appear to come from a single provider, but it depends on a supply chain of AI chips, power, cooling, networks, facilities and financing. Because the value chain runs from chipmaker to end user, a problem at any point can cascade. A chip shortage, power constraint, platform outage or financing problem can quickly spread beyond the immediate point of failure. Constraints and issues can propagate downstream into higher latency, degraded service, missed service levels and, eventually, lost trust by end users. GPUaaS needs to appropriately address such resilience issues.

...

Against that backdrop, GPUaaS has several economic features: 

1. Capital intensity: a meaningful GPU cluster is a large upfront investment that depreciates quickly and carries real obsolescence risk.
2. Operational complexity: modern AI infrastructure requires power, cooling, high-speed networking, orchestration and specialist engineering, as well as GPUs.
3. Procurement risk: advanced GPUs have at times been difficult to obtain, with lead times extending well beyond ordinary technology cycles. Renting can, in some circumstances, compress deployment times from months to days.
4. Utilisation: idle GPUs consume capital, so an outsourcing model provides flexibility and transfers utilisation risk to the provider.

...

2. Migration of value up the stack. ... The question for suppliers is whether durable margins and value sits in the infrastructure itself or in the managed services, orchestration, model hosting and inference platforms built on top of it.
